sections.title: Universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals: a common challenge for all countries

summary.text: Explains why a health workforce of adequate size, skill mix, and distribution is essential for achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and the health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and why comprehensive workforce data are needed to address shortages and labour market imbalances.

sections.extract: Development Goals: a common challenge for all countries A health workforce (HWF) of adequate size and skill mix, as well as required teachers and trainers, are critical to the attainment of any population health goal. This includes the achieve- ment of universal health coverage (UHC) (WHO 2017c) and the health-related targets of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Yet countries globally are

summary.text: Summarizes the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 (adopted under resolution WHA69.19), highlighting its four objectives, global milestones for 2020 and 2030, and call for progressive implementation of National Health Workforce Accounts.

sections.title: Benefits of the National Health Workforce Accounts
Benefits at the global level

summary.text: Outlines the global-level benefits of the NHWA in standardizing health workforce information systems for interoperability, supporting monitoring of the GSHRH and SDG targets, and streamlining international data reporting across WHO, OECD, and Eurostat.

sections.extract: From the Action Plan of the High-Level Commission, and specifically the GSHRH, the concept of NHWA is clearly promoted as an important means to support countries in their national HWF policy and planning. The Sixty-ninth World Health Assembly adopted resolution WHA69.19 in support of its implementation(World Health Assembly 2016). The purpose of the NHWA is to facilitate the standardization of health workforce

sections.title: Benefits at the national level

summary.text: Describes the national-level benefits of implementing the NHWA as a flexible, modular framework tailored to country policy priorities, accompanied by five guiding principles on country ownership, multisectoral governance, progressive strengthening of HRHIS, data security, and alignment with existing systems.

sections.extract: The NHWA indicators have been selected with clear policy relevance in mind, so that they can be used by any country according to its own specific needs. While designed to support a coherent framework for HWF policy analysis and design, the NHWA can be implemented and used in a flexible, modular way. It is important for countries to note that while the 10 NHWA modules provide full coverage of indicators for all

sections.title: Benefits at the regional level

summary.text: Highlights the regional-level benefits of the NHWA in improving cross-country comparability of health workforce data, tracking bilateral and multilateral mobility, and supporting regional observatories and economic integration agreements.

sections.extract: Apart from the benefits at national level, the NHWA can also ease the comparability of the HWF landscape at regional level and globally. Through country reporting and international compar- isons, the NHWA may facilitate cross-country capacity-building, information and knowledge exchange, as well as more sophisticated research about future trends of health workforces within and across systems.

sections.title: The underpinning framework

summary.text: Presents the health labour market framework underpinning the NHWA (Figure 1), showing how education pipelines and labour market dynamics interact under four core policy domains—production, inflows and outflows, maldistribution and inefficiencies, and private-sector regulation—to achieve universal health coverage.

sections.extract: The concept of the NHWA is closely aligned with the health labour market framework for UHC (Sousa et al. 2013) (Figure 1), which also takes a central place in the High-Level Commission’s report ‘Working for health and growth: investing in the health workforce’(High-Level Commis- sion on Health Employment and Economic 2016). This framework provides a comprehensive picture of the education sector and health labour

sections.title: A modular approach

summary.text: Describes the modular architecture of the NHWA (Figure 2), organizing 78 core indicators across 10 modules that span health workforce education (Modules 2–4), the active labour force (Modules 1 and 5–7), and serving population health needs (Modules 8–10).

sections.extract: A modular approach The NHWA contains a set of 78 core indicators, spread over 10 modules, that aim to support national-level HWF policies to progress towards UHC and SDGs. The indicators in the 10 modules feed into three crucial labour market components: the education component, the labour force component and the component serving population health needs (Figure 2). Figure 2: Overview of labour market components

sections.title: Implementation of the NHWA

summary.text: Emphasizes that NHWA implementation is a country-led, intersectoral process building on existing national and subnational health workforce databases, supported by the WHO NHWA online platform, implementation guide, and regional training workshops.

sections.extract: The NHWA contains indicators with clear policy relevance across the entire spectrum of HWF priorities and those related to the health labour market framework. The implementation of the NHWA is a country-led activity, building on national systems and using existing mechanisms to coordinate data-gathering for the evaluation of the health workforce. WHO has developed a set of tools to help countries implement the NHWA.

sections.title: Potential use of the NHWA

summary.text: Notes that the NHWA combines quantitative numeric indicators and qualitative capability indicators to support national policy-making, pointing to worked policy applications in Annex 3.

sections.extract: As described in the metadata sheets, the NHWA includes both numeric and ‘capability’ indica- tors that provide information on regulation and other mechanisms related to the health work- force. Tangible examples on what implementation of the NHWA can mean for countries, and how it can support them in policy-making at national level, are provided in Annex 3. sections.title: Methodological note on implementation

summary.text: Provides methodological guidance for implementing NHWA indicators, covering annual measurement periods, public/private sector and subnational disaggregation, health workforce occupation classifications (ISCO-08) and activity status categories (practising, professionally active, licensed), and major national data sources.

sections.extract: Annual measurement The monitoring of indicators in the NHWA is expected to occur on annual basis, although more regular monitoring schemes are possible. This implies reporting on indicators to cover a period of one year. Where data reporting is expected less regularly, this is marked in the individual indicator descriptive sheets. summary.text: Describes in Annex 1 the multiphase consultative process used from 2015 to 2017 to filter over 450 candidate metrics down to 78 core NHWA indicators through Technical Advisory Group reviews, expert scoring on relevance and feasibility, and global public consultation.

sections.extract: the National Health Workforce Accounts National Health Workforce Accounts: A Handbook The list of National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) indicators was developed through a stepwise process that included several phases of consultation on preselected indicators. summary.text: Explains in Annex 2 the structure and fields of the Part II indicator metadata sheets, defining indicator numbering, numerator and denominator specifications, disaggregation categories, capability scoring questions, data reporting frequency, and potential data sources.

sections.extract: National Health Workforce Accounts: A Handbook The indicators in the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) are specified in the metadata sheets outlined in Part II of this Handbook. The indicators are mostly numeric (quantitative), i.e. representing in numbers certain ratios with a numerator and denominator related to a human resources for health (HRH) policy field.
